question.text:
Consider the following matrices:

\[ B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $B = PDP^{-1},$ find $\ln B.$
question.explanation:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have \[ f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}. \]

For $f(x) = \ln x$ and the given matrix $B,$ we have

\[ \ln B = \ln(PDP^{-1}) = P \cdot (\ln D) \cdot P^{-1}. \]

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

\[ \ln D = \begin{bmatrix} \ln 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \ln 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \ln 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

\[ P^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2\cdot1 - 1\cdot1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \ln B &= P \cdot (\ln D) \cdot P^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \ln 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ -\ln 2 & 2\ln 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\ln 2 & 2\ln 2 \\ -\ln 2 & 2\ln 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the following matrices:

\[ Y = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ - 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad J = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $Y = PJP^{-1},$ find $2^Y.$
question.explanation:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have \[ f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}. \]

For $f(x) = 2^x$ and the given matrix $Y,$ we have

\[ 2^Y = 2^{PJP^{-1}} = P \cdot (2^J) \cdot P^{-1}. \]

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $1$s on the main diagonal, we have

\[ f(J) = \begin{bmatrix} f(1) & f'(1) \\ 0 & f(1) \end{bmatrix}. \]

The derivative of $f$ is $f'(x) = 2^x\ln x.$ So, we get

\[ 2^J = \begin{bmatrix} f(1) & f'(1) \\ 0 & f(1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2^1 & 2^1\ln2 \\ 0 & 2^1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2\ln2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

\[ P^{-1} = \dfrac{2}{1\cdot1 - 1\cdot1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\begin{align*} 2^Y &= P \cdot (2^J) \cdot P^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2\ln2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2-2\ln2 & -2+4\ln2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2-4\ln2 & 8\ln2 \\ -2\ln2 & 2+4\ln2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

First, note that

\begin{align*} (J_2(2) {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} J_2(3))^3 &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} J_2(2) & 0 \\ 0 & J_2(3) \end{bmatrix} \right)^3 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} (J_2(2))^3 & 0 \\ 0 & (J_2(3))^3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (J_2(2))^3 {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} (J_2(3))^3. \end{align*}

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

  • For $J_2(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=2.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only: \begin{align*} f(x) &= {x}^3 \\[5pt] f'(x) &= 3x^2 \end{align*} So, we get \begin{align*} f(J_2(2)) &= \begin{bmatrix} f(2) & f'(2) \\ 0 & f(2) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2^3 & 3\cdot 2^2 \\ 0 & 2^3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 12 \\ 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

  • For $J_2(3),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=3.$ Since $n=2,$ we need the first derivative of $f$ only, which we have already computed. So, we get \begin{align*} f(J_2(3)) &= \begin{bmatrix} f(3) & f'(3) \\ 0 & f(3) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3^3 & 3\cdot 3^2 \\ 0 & 3^3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 27 & 27 \\ 0 & 27 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
